lines.text: On {26 December 2004|the twenty-sixth of December, two thousand four}, a magnitude {9.1|nine point one} earthquake broke the seafloor off Sumatra.
The tsunami took {2 hours 36 minutes|two hours and thirty-six minutes} to reach Chennai, and almost three hours to reach Colombo.
The Indian Ocean had no warning system. More than {227,000|two hundred and twenty-seven thousand} people died.
This is {LeadTime|Leed Time}. It asks one question: how many minutes does a coastal city get to run?
Replay 2004, and a shallow-water solver carries the wave across the real ocean floor, {live|lyve} in your browser.
Over deep water it moves as fast as a jet, and twelve hours of tsunami play out in under a minute.
The seafloor bends it into beams. Here's where it hit hardest, and when, hour by hour.
For {65|sixty-five} cities on the coast, you see when the wave arrives, and how many people live there.
With no sensors, nobody gets a confirmed warning.
Now you're the engineer. Drop one deep-ocean sensor west of Sumatra, and {73.1 million|seventy-three point one million} people get at least fifteen minutes to evacuate.
Chennai, with {6.7 million|six point seven million} people, gets {101|a hundred and one} minutes.
The optimizer tests {15|fifteen} possible earthquakes along the trenches, and places six sensors.
The first warns about {53 million|fifty-three million} people per quake. The sixth adds nothing.
Real networks also weigh cost and upkeep, but now you can see what each sensor buys.
And the honest part: Banda Aceh is hit in {21|twenty-one} minutes. No sensor can save it.
On nearby Simeulue Island, an oral tradition did. Only seven of more than {78,000|seventy-eight thousand} people died there.
Can you trust the physics? Against {13|thirteen} tide gauges from 2004, our arrival times are off by {20|twenty} minutes on average, and mostly early.
So the warning times you see err on the safe side.
{LeadTime|Leed Time}. Free, open source, no login. Every minute counts.
